summary: Describes an architecture for a global, scalable and distributed system that maps a geographic location to a URL, using the LoST protocol. It draws on hierarchical lookup ideas similar to DNS. Emergency services are an example of where such lookups matter.

plainLanguage.summary: Like a phone book that tells you which fire station is nearest, this system turns where you are into the web address of the right service for that place.

questions: how does lost map location to url
what is a forest guide in lost
subtitle: A DNS-like hierarchy of servers that turns where you are into the URL of the right local service, such as emergency help.

tldr.problem: Services such as emergency calling are offered by many local providers, and the right one depends on the caller's location, so a global system must map a location to a service URL.
tldr.mechanism: Seekers ask resolvers, which consult forest guides that know the coverage regions of trees, which are hierarchies of authoritative mapping servers. All of them talk LoST.
tldr.outcome: The design allows authority to be distributed among many independent operators without a single global root. It is an Informational architecture document.

facts.label: Expected number of trees
facts.value: A few hundred to a few thousand (author's guess)

facts.label: Tree coverage change rate
facts.value: Less than one change per year per tree (assumed)

today: RFC 5582 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an architecture built on LoST (RFC 5222) and does not define a new protocol.

sections.title: The Mapping Problem
sections.content:
Many services are offered by local providers, so the provider you need depends on where you are. Emergency calling is the best-known case, since calls go to the most appropriate public safety answering point (PSAP) for the caller's physical location. Food delivery, directory services and roadside assistance follow the same pattern.

This is a mapping problem: a geographic location and a service identifier are translated into a set of service URIs. The RFC describes an architecture for a global, scalable and resilient system that does this. It uses the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol (RFC 5222), although much of the discussion would apply to other mapping protocols. The architecture lets operators combine and split functions freely and imposes few requirements on who runs what.
sections.plainLanguage: Which fire station helps you depends on where you are standing. This system looks at your spot and tells you the right address to contact.

sections.title: Seekers, Resolvers, Trees and Forest Guides
sections.content:
The architecture has four logical roles. A seeker is a LoST client that asks for a mapping. A resolver caches earlier answers and knows how to reach forest guides. A forest guide (FG) knows the coverage regions of trees. A tree is a hierarchy of authoritative mapping servers (AMS) that hold the real mapping data. All of them speak LoST, and a synchronization protocol can exchange information between forest guides or push coverage up a tree.

The collection of trees is called a forest. The author guesses there will be between a few hundred and a few thousand trees, depending on whether each country runs one or independent organizations run their own. Tree coverage is assumed to change less than once per year per tree. A minimal system with only seekers and resolvers is possible, but is compared to the old hosts.txt approach and is unlikely to scale globally.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask a helper, the helper asks a guide who knows which region belongs to which map, and that map's keeper gives you the final answer.

sections.title: How Trees Answer Queries
sections.content:
A tree node represents a geographic area and points to child nodes for smaller areas. Each node can be a cluster of LoST servers that hold the same information and back each other up. Nodes hold two kinds of data: coverage regions, which point to a child server, and mappings, which hold the actual service URI. Leaf nodes hold only mappings, and nodes above them hold only coverage regions. Regions can be geometric shapes or sets of civic address parts such as country = DE, A1 = Bavaria, and need not follow political boundaries.

A node answers by forwarding the query down the tree and returning the response (recursion), or by returning the child's server name to the querier (iteration). A node may return a whole region with a time-to-live instead of a single point answer, so the querier can cache it. If coverage regions overlap, the node returns all answers in redirection mode or queries both children in recursive mode.

The tree is described as roughly similar to DNS, except that delegation is by region rather than by label.
sections.plainLanguage: Big maps point to smaller maps, until one small map says "for your street, call this station". You can remember the answer for the whole neighbourhood.

sections.title: Forest Guides, Caching and Service Numbers
sections.content:
Forest guides keep track of the coverage regions of all trees for one service and location profile. They redirect and do not give mapping answers themselves. They resemble DNS root servers, but avoid a single global root, and they may offer different information according to local policy. For example, if country C does not recognize country T, C can propagate tree regions for all but T. Peering between forest guides implies trust and so is likely to need negotiation between the operators.

Seekers and resolvers cache results. Because answers can describe a whole region, a mobile user usually needs to look up service areas only once per cache lifetime along a regular route, and the RFC mentions cache lifetimes of several days. The architecture can also deliver local service numbers such as 9-1-1 in North America and 1-1-2 in Europe, since more than 60 emergency numbers are in use around the world. Systems should be able to find both the home and the visited country's numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Guides keep a list of who is in charge of each area. Your device remembers answers for a few days, and the system can also tell travellers what the local emergency number is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Server impersonation is handled with the underlying channel security, such as TLS. To stop tampering with queries or results, the architecture RECOMMENDS channel security and says results SHOULD also be digitally signed, for example with XML digital signatures. A signature alone does not prove that the signer may speak for a geographic area, so well-known Certificate Authorities might need to vet mapping sources.

Any node that introduces a new service boundary MUST sign the object, and a recipient MUST check through local policy that the signer is authorized for that region. Receivers should be especially suspicious if an existing coverage region is replaced by one with a new mapping address. In many cases trust is mediated: a seeker trusts its resolver, and the resolver trusts forest guides. Denial-of-service attacks are left to operational measures.
sections.plainLanguage: Because people rely on these answers in emergencies, the answers must be signed so nobody can fake a map or claim an area that is not theirs.
